events.title: Theodoric the Amal seizes Dyrrachium
events.summary: Frustrated by Zeno's broken promises, Theodoric marched his Goths west in 479 and seized Dyrrachium on the Adriatic by a ruse. The envoy Adamantius offered lands in Dardania; while talks went on, the general Sabinianus ambushed the Gothic rearguard under Theodimund and captured 2,000 wagons and 5,000 prisoners. Malchus's account of the negotiations is unusually detailed.

events.title: Revolt of Marcian in Constantinople
events.summary: Marcian, son of the western emperor Anthemius and husband of Ariadne's sister Leontia, claimed the throne in late 479, arguing that Leontia, born after Leo I's accession, had a better right than Ariadne. His men nearly took the palace, but Illus brought Isaurian troops across from Chalcedon overnight; Marcian was ordained a priest and exiled to Cappadocia.

events.title: Death of Theodoric Strabo
events.summary: After a failed attack on Constantinople in 481, Theodoric Strabo marched into Greece and was killed when his rearing horse threw him onto a spear hanging by his tent. His son Recitach was murdered by Theodoric the Amal in 484, who absorbed Strabo's Goths and became the sole leader of the Balkan Goths.

events.title: Sabas founds the Great Lavra
events.summary: The Cappadocian monk Sabas founded the Great Lavra in the gorge of the Kidron between Jerusalem and the Dead Sea in 483. It became the leading monastery of Palestine and a stronghold of Chalcedonian orthodoxy; Sabas twice travelled to Constantinople as spokesman of the Palestinian monks. The monastery is still inhabited.

events.title: Death of Peroz against the Hephthalites
events.summary: Peroz I, who had already been captured once by the Hephthalites and ransomed, invaded their territory again in 484 and was killed with most of his army and several sons when his cavalry charged into a concealed trench. Procopius tells that he threw away his famous pearl earring as he fell. Persia paid tribute to the Hephthalites for years, a weakness that drove Kavad's demands for Roman gold.

battle.significance: Worst Sasanian defeat before the Arab conquest.

events.title: Odoacer destroys the Rugian kingdom
events.summary: In 487 Odoacer crossed the Danube against the Rugians of King Feletheus (Feva), whose son Fredericus had murdered his uncle. He captured Feletheus and Queen Giso, brought them to Italy and executed them. Fredericus fled to Theodoric, and in 488 Odoacer ordered the Roman population of Noricum evacuated to Italy.

events.title: Zeno closes the School of the Persians at Edessa
events.summary: Zeno ordered the closure in 489 of the 'School of the Persians' at Edessa, a centre of Antiochene, Theodoran theology. Its teachers, led by Narsai who had already moved to Nisibis, re-established it across the frontier. The School of Nisibis became the intellectual centre of the Church of the East and transmitted Greek learning in Syriac.

sources.w: Cause of the Foundation of the Schools

events.title: Deposition and restoration of Kavad I
events.summary: Kavad I, who backed the egalitarian preaching of Mazdak, was deposed by the nobles and priests in 496 and imprisoned in the 'Castle of Oblivion'. Escaping with his wife's help, he fled to the Hephthalites, married a Hephthalite princess and returned with an army in 498 or 499 to oust his brother Zamasp. Needing money to pay his allies, he demanded Roman subsidies and invaded in 502.

events.title: End of the Isaurian War
events.summary: The last Isaurian strongholds fell in 497-498; Longinus of Selinus and Indes were captured and paraded in chains in Constantinople and Longinus was tortured to death at Nicaea. Many Isaurians were resettled in Thrace. Anastasius commemorated the victory with a hymn sung in the Hippodrome.

events.title: Bulgars defeat the Illyrian army on the Tzurta
events.summary: In 499 Bulgars raiding Thrace annihilated an army of 15,000 under Aristus, magister militum per Illyricum, at the river Tzurta; Marcellinus Comes says more than 4,000 Romans died, including four named comites. It is one of the first recorded Bulgar victories over the empire and spurred Anastasius to build the Long Walls.

events.title: Battle of Dijon
events.summary: Allied with Godegisel, who betrayed his brother, Clovis defeated the Burgundian king Gundobad near Dijon on the Ouche in 500. Gundobad fled to Avignon and survived a siege by agreeing to pay tribute, then in 501 recovered and killed Godegisel at Vienne. The Burgundian kingdom survived another three decades.

battle.significance: Burgundy made tributary for a time.

events.title: The Edictum Theoderici
events.summary: A collection of 154 short articles applying Roman law, much of it drawn from the Theodosian Code and Pauli Sententiae, to Goths and Romans alike. It survives only in Pierre Pithou's edition of 1579, the manuscripts having been lost, and is traditionally attributed to Theodoric the Great around 500-512.
events.debate: Piero Rasi argued in 1953 that it was issued by the Visigothic king Theoderic II in Gaul; the question is unresolved.

events.title: Theodoric's palace church: Sant'Apollinare Nuovo
events.summary: Theodoric built an Arian palace church dedicated to Christ the Redeemer in Ravenna around 505, with mosaics of the life of Christ and a depiction of his palace and Classe. After the reconquest Archbishop Agnellus rededicated it to St Martin (c. 561) and replaced the Gothic court figures with processions of martyrs and virgins; hands of the erased figures still show on the palace columns.

events.title: Council of Agde
events.summary: In September 506 the Arian king Alaric II allowed 35 Catholic bishops of his kingdom to meet at Agde under Caesarius of Arles, months after promulgating the Breviary. Its 48 canons on clerical discipline, property and marriage became standard in Gallic church law. Vouillé followed a year later.

events.title: Ostrogoths relieve Arles
events.summary: After Vouillé, Franks and Burgundians besieged Arles in 507-508; Bishop Caesarius was suspected of treason. Theodoric sent an army under Ibba and Tuluin that lifted the siege; Jordanes claims 30,000 Franks died. Provence became an Ostrogothic province governed by a praetorian prefect of the Gauls, and Theodoric saved Septimania for the Visigoths.

battle.significance: Created Ostrogothic Provence and checked Clovis.

events.title: Pactus Legis Salicae
events.summary: Issued under Clovis around 507-511, the Salic Law set out in 65 titles the compensations (wergild) for crimes among the Franks: 200 solidi for killing a free Frank, 100 for a Roman landowner, 600 for a royal follower. Its Malberg glosses preserve Frankish legal words. A clause on inheritance of land was later invoked to bar women from the French throne.

events.title: Theodoric becomes regent of the Visigoths
events.summary: After Ibba's army drove out the Visigothic king Gesalec in 511, Theodoric ruled the Visigothic kingdom as guardian of his grandson Amalaric, Alaric II's son, until 526, governing through the Ostrogoth Theudis and sending Visigothic treasure to Ravenna. For fifteen years one king ruled from the Danube to the Atlantic.

events.title: Anastasius deposes Patriarch Macedonius II
events.summary: Patriarch Macedonius II of Constantinople, who refused to anathematise Chalcedon, was deposed and exiled in August 511 after being accused of heresy and immorality; Anastasius installed Timothy I. The crowds of the capital, largely Chalcedonian, never forgave the emperor and rioted over the Trisagion in 512.

events.title: Severus becomes patriarch of Antioch
events.summary: In November 512, after a synod at Sidon and the deposition of Flavian II, Anastasius made the brilliant anti-Chalcedonian monk and former Beirut law student Severus patriarch of Antioch. His theology defined the miaphysite position; deposed by Justin I in 518, he fled to Egypt and remained the movement's leading thinker.

events.title: Vitalian routs Hypatius and captures him
events.summary: In the first year of his rebellion, Vitalian defeated the army of Anastasius's nephew Hypatius near Odessus on the Black Sea coast and captured him; Hypatius was later ransomed. The defeat forced Anastasius to negotiate and promise a church council, which he never honoured.

events.title: The Burgundian Liber Constitutionum
events.summary: Promulgated by King Sigismund at Lyon on 29 March 517, the Liber Constitutionum (Lex Gundobada) compiled laws of his father Gundobad regulating relations between Burgundians and Romans, including the division of estates with 'guests' (hospites). A separate Lex Romana Burgundionum applied Roman law to the Roman population.

events.title: Mausoleum of Theodoric
events.summary: Built c. 520 outside Ravenna's walls, Theodoric's two-storey decagonal tomb of Istrian limestone is roofed by a single monolith about 10 m across and weighing some 230 tonnes, with twelve pierced handles used to set it in place. The Anonymus Valesianus says Theodoric had a great stone found to cover it. His porphyry bathtub-sarcophagus now stands inside, empty.

events.title: Revolt and flight of Gourgenes of Iberia
events.summary: When Kavad tried to impose Zoroastrian rites, including exposure of the dead, on Christian Iberia, King Gourgenes appealed to Justin I, who sent only a small force. Gourgenes and his nobles fled to Lazica and then Constantinople. The episode opened the Iberian war of 526-532.

events.title: Boethius writes the Consolation of Philosophy
events.summary: Condemned without trial for treason, Boethius wrote the Consolation of Philosophy in prison near Pavia in 524, a dialogue in alternating prose and verse in which Lady Philosophy leads him from self-pity to the knowledge of providence and the true good. Translated by Alfred the Great, Chaucer and Elizabeth I, it was among the most read books of the Middle Ages.

events.title: Dionysius Exiguus introduces the Anno Domini era
events.summary: Asked by Pope John I to calculate Easter dates, the Scythian monk Dionysius Exiguus in Rome produced in 525 a table for 532-626 in which he replaced Diocletian's era, named after a persecutor, with years counted from the Incarnation. Bede's use of the system in the eighth century spread the Anno Domini count across the Latin West.

events.title: Execution of Symmachus
events.summary: Quintus Aurelius Memmius Symmachus, head of the Senate, historian and Boethius's father-in-law and guardian, was taken to Ravenna and executed in 525 or 526, fearing, says the Anonymus Valesianus, that grief for Boethius would drive him to plot. Procopius links Theodoric's remorse for these deaths to his own end.

events.title: Kavad's request that Justin adopt Khosrow
events.summary: Seeking to secure his favourite son's succession, Kavad asked Justin I around 525 to adopt Khosrow. The quaestor Proclus warned that adoption could give Khosrow a claim to the Roman empire, and Justin offered only adoption 'by arms', as among barbarians. The insult wrecked talks at the frontier, the Persian negotiator Seoses was executed, and war followed.

events.title: Priscian's Institutes of Grammar
events.summary: Priscian of Caesarea in Mauretania, teaching Latin in Constantinople, wrote the Institutiones Grammaticae in 18 books around 500-526, the largest Latin grammar from antiquity, quoting hundreds of passages from classical authors. A copy was made by the palace scribe Flavius Theodorus in 526-527; it became the standard medieval grammar.

events.title: Pope John I sent to Constantinople
events.summary: Theodoric forced Pope John I to lead an embassy to Justin I in 525-526 to obtain the restoration of churches confiscated from Arians in the East. John was received with unprecedented honours and celebrated Easter in Hagia Sophia, but secured only part of his brief. On his return Theodoric imprisoned him at Ravenna, where he died on 18 May 526.

events.title: Church of Saints Sergius and Bacchus
events.summary: Built by Justinian and Theodora c. 527-536 beside the palace of Hormisdas, the octagon-in-a-square church of Sergius and Bacchus, with its carved inscription praising 'God-crowned Theodora', anticipated Hagia Sophia's domed central plan. It survives as the Küçük Ayasofya mosque.

events.title: Massacre of the Mazdakites
events.summary: Late in Kavad's reign, around 528, Prince Khosrow, the designated heir, invited Mazdak and his followers to a debate or banquet and had them massacred; tradition says they were buried alive head down. The suppression of the Mazdakite movement, which had preached communal property and women, was followed by Khosrow's reconstruction of noble estates and taxation.
events.debate: Dates range from 524 to 531; much of the story is romance.

events.title: Justinian makes al-Harith supreme phylarch
events.summary: After the Lakhmid al-Mundhir III raided as far as Antioch, Justinian conferred on al-Harith ibn Jabala of the Ghassanid (Jafnid) family 'the dignity of king' over the Arab federates of the eastern provinces around 529. The Ghassanids became Rome's principal desert shield and, as Miaphysites, patrons of the anti-Chalcedonian church.

events.title: Gelimer deposes Hilderic
events.summary: Hilderic, grandson of Valentinian III through Eudocia, had ended persecution of Catholics and favoured Justinian. In June 530 his cousin Gelimer, leader of the Vandal war party after a defeat by the Moors, deposed and imprisoned him. Justinian's demand for Hilderic's restoration was rejected, giving the pretext for the Vandal war.

events.title: The Fifty Decisions
events.summary: In 530-531, in preparation for the Digest, Justinian issued a series of constitutions, the Quinquaginta decisiones, settling long-standing controversies among the classical jurists, for instance on legacies and freeing slaves. They were later absorbed into the second edition of the Code in 534.

events.title: Romanos the Melode and the kontakion
events.summary: Romanos, a Syrian deacon from Emesa serving at the church of the Theotokos in Kyros in Constantinople, composed some 80 surviving kontakia, long metrical sermons sung with refrains. His hymn On Earthquakes and Fires reflects the Nika riot and the rebuilding of Hagia Sophia and praises Justinian; tradition credits him with a thousand hymns.

events.title: Justinian's Theopaschite edict
events.summary: On 15 March 533 Justinian issued an edict affirming that 'one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh', a formula championed by Scythian monks that he hoped would reconcile Chalcedonians and Miaphysites. Pope John II accepted it in 534; it was a first step in the policy that led to the condemnation of the Three Chapters.

events.title: Battle of Mammes
events.summary: Solomon, left in command of Africa after Belisarius's departure, attacked a Moorish army in Byzacena at Mammes in 534. The Moors formed a circle of camels twelve deep to protect their women and children; Solomon's dismounted men broke into the ring and Procopius claims 10,000 Moors were killed.

battle.significance: First test of Roman Africa against the Moors.

events.title: Battle of Mount Bourgaon
events.summary: In 535 the Moors of Byzacena regrouped on Mount Bourgaon. Solomon sent a force under Theodorus to climb the far side by night; attacked from above, the Moors fled down the slopes into the main Roman army. Procopius claims 50,000 Moors died without a Roman loss, an obvious exaggeration.

battle.significance: Pacified Byzacena until the mutiny of 536.

events.title: Pope Agapetus deposes Anthimus; Synod of 536
events.summary: Sent by Theodahad to avert war, Pope Agapetus arrived in Constantinople in February 536 and persuaded Justinian, over Theodora's objections, to depose the patriarch Anthimus as a crypto-Miaphysite. Agapetus consecrated Menas and died in the capital on 22 April. A synod in May-June 536 condemned Anthimus and Severus of Antioch, whose books Justinian ordered burned.

events.title: Witiges elected king; Theodahad killed
events.summary: Disgusted with Theodahad's inaction as Belisarius took Naples, the Gothic army raised the veteran officer Witiges on a shield at Regata near Terracina in November 536. Theodahad fled toward Ravenna and was killed on the road by a personal enemy. Witiges married Amalasuntha's daughter Matasuntha to gain Amal legitimacy.

events.title: Battle of Scalae Veteres
events.summary: Justinian's cousin Germanus, sent to deal with the mutiny of Stotzas in Africa, won back much of the army by paying arrears and in spring 537 defeated the mutineers and their Moorish allies at Scalae Veteres in Numidia. Stotzas fled to Mauretania.

events.title: Belisarius deposes Pope Silverius
events.summary: During the siege of Rome, Pope Silverius was accused of offering to open the Asinarian Gate to the Goths. In March 537 Belisarius and Antonina had him stripped of his pallium and replaced by the deacon Vigilius, Theodora's candidate. Silverius died in exile on the island of Palmaria later that year.

events.title: Siege of Ariminum
events.summary: John, nephew of Vitalian, seized Ariminum against Belisarius's orders in 538, drawing Witiges away from Rome. Besieged, he refused to withdraw; the newly arrived Narses persuaded Belisarius to relieve him and the Goths fled at the sight of the converging armies. The episode began the quarrel between Narses and Belisarius.

events.title: Siege of Auximum
events.summary: Belisarius besieged the strongly sited Gothic garrison of Auximum (Osimo) in the Marche for some seven months in 539, fouling its only water cistern with corpses and quicklime. The garrison surrendered late in the year and many enrolled in the Roman army, opening the road to Ravenna.

events.title: Theudebert invades Italy
events.summary: In 539 the Frankish king Theudebert I, courted by both sides, crossed the Alps with an army Procopius numbers at 100,000, slaughtered the Goths at the bridge of Ticinum and then the Romans, and plundered Liguria until dysentery killed a third of his men. He later struck gold coins in his own name, an affront Procopius noted.

events.title: The Rule of Saint Benedict
events.summary: Around 540 Benedict of Nursia composed at Monte Cassino a Rule in 73 chapters, drawing heavily on the anonymous Rule of the Master, that organised monks' lives under an abbot around the divine office, manual labour and reading, with moderation in food and sleep. Promoted by the Carolingians, it became the standard rule of western monasticism.

events.title: Gildas's On the Ruin of Britain
events.summary: Written in Britain probably in the 530s or 540s, Gildas's De Excidio Britanniae denounces five British kings and the clergy as sinners whose vices invited the Saxon conquest. Its historical prologue, with the 'groans of the Britons', the 'proud tyrant' who invited the Saxons and the victory at Mount Badon, is the only British narrative of the fifth century.
events.debate: Datings range from the 480s to the 540s.

events.title: Theodora's Miaphysite mission to Nobatia
events.summary: John of Ephesus relates that around 543 Theodora sent the priest Julian to convert the Nubian kingdom of Nobatia to Miaphysite Christianity, ordering the governor of the Thebaid to delay a rival Chalcedonian mission sent by Justinian. Julian arrived first; the Nobadian king and nobles were baptised and Nubia's church remained Miaphysite.

events.title: The Nea church in Jerusalem
events.summary: Justinian's church of Mary Mother of God, the Nea, was dedicated on 20 November 543 on the slope of Mount Zion, its platform carried on vast vaults. Procopius describes columns quarried locally because none could be brought; an inscription found in its cistern in 1977 names Justinian and the abbot Constantine. The Madaba map shows it at the end of the cardo.

events.title: Edict against the Three Chapters
events.summary: To win over the Miaphysites, Justinian condemned in 543-544 the 'Three Chapters': the person and works of Theodore of Mopsuestia, Theodoret's writings against Cyril, and the letter of Ibas of Edessa to Mari, all associated with Chalcedon. Western bishops saw an attack on the council; the African and Italian churches refused, and Pope Vigilius was summoned to Constantinople.

events.title: Fortified monastery of Mount Sinai
events.summary: Between about 548 and 565 Justinian built a fortified monastery of the Theotokos at the foot of Mount Sinai around the site of the Burning Bush, with a garrison to protect the monks from Saracen raids. Its basilica's apse mosaic of the Transfiguration, dated by inscription, and its icons, including the sixth-century encaustic Christ Pantokrator, survive in situ.

events.title: Abraha repairs the Marib dam and receives four embassies
events.summary: A long Sabaic inscription (CIH 541) records that the Aksumite ruler of Himyar, Abraha, put down a revolt and repaired the great dam of Marib in 548, and received envoys from the Negus of Aksum, the Roman emperor, the King of Kings, al-Harith the Ghassanid and al-Mundhir the Lakhmid. It shows Yemen as a node of great-power diplomacy.

events.title: The Iudicatum of Vigilius
events.summary: Brought to Constantinople in 547, Pope Vigilius issued on 11 April 548 a judgement (Iudicatum) condemning the Three Chapters while affirming Chalcedon. The western backlash was so fierce, with African bishops excommunicating him, that Justinian let him withdraw it in 550; Vigilius was later dragged from a church altar and twice fled to sanctuary.

events.title: Corippus's Iohannis
events.summary: Flavius Cresconius Corippus, an African grammarian, recited at Carthage around 549-550 a Latin epic in eight books on John Troglita's campaigns against the Moors of 546-548. Its ethnographic catalogues of Moorish tribes and descriptions of their camel laagers and rites are unique.

events.title: Cosmas Indicopleustes's Christian Topography
events.summary: An Alexandrian merchant who had sailed to Aksum and the Red Sea, known as Cosmas Indicopleustes ('sailor to India'), wrote c. 550 a treatise arguing that the universe has the shape of the Tabernacle with a flat earth. His digressions preserve invaluable observations on Aksum, the inscription of Adulis, the trade of Taprobane (Sri Lanka) and Indian Ocean commerce.

events.title: Slav invasion of 550
events.summary: In 550 a large Sclavene army crossed the Danube, approached Naissus intending to attack Thessalonica, then turned east, defeated an imperial army near Adrianople and raided to the Long Walls. Germanus's army gathering at Serdica for Italy deterred them for a time. Procopius describes their savagery in detail.

battle.significance: Showed that Slav raiders could beat field armies.

events.title: Church of the Holy Apostles rebuilt
events.summary: Justinian replaced Constantine's church of the Holy Apostles with a cruciform church of five domes, dedicated on 28 June 550, adjoining the mausoleum of Constantine where emperors were buried until 1028. Its design inspired San Marco in Venice; the church was demolished after 1461 for the Fatih Mosque.

events.title: Procopius publishes the Wars
events.summary: Procopius of Caesarea, Belisarius's assessor, published Books 1-7 of his History of the Wars, on the Persian, Vandal and Gothic campaigns, around 550-551, adding Book 8 in 553-554. Modelled on Thucydides and Herodotus, it is the last great classical history and the main source for Justinian's wars.

events.title: Siege of Archaeopolis
events.summary: The Persian general Mermeroes attacked Archaeopolis, the strongest fortress of Lazica, in 551 with elephants and Sabir Huns. The Roman garrison sallied, a wounded elephant panicked the Persian ranks and Mermeroes withdrew with about 4,000 dead.

events.title: Earthquake and tsunami at Berytus
events.summary: On 9 July 551 a great earthquake struck the Levantine coast, destroying Berytus, where Agathias says thousands died including many foreign law students, and causing a tsunami. The famous law school moved to Sidon and never recovered its former standing.

events.title: Schism of the Three Chapters in northern Italy
events.summary: When Vigilius and his successor Pelagius I accepted the condemnation of the Three Chapters by the council of 553, the metropolitans of Aquileia and Milan broke communion with Rome. The Aquileian schism, sheltered after 568 by the Lombards, lasted until the Synod of Pavia in 698 and split the patriarchate into Grado and Aquileia.

events.title: Cassiodorus founds Vivarium
events.summary: Returning from Constantinople after the Gothic war, Cassiodorus founded the monastery of Vivarium, named after its fishponds, on his family estates at Squillace in Bruttium. For its monks he wrote the Institutiones (c. 562), a guide to sacred and secular reading, and organised a scriptorium to copy and correct texts, making manuscript copying a monastic duty.

events.title: Roman generals murder King Gubazes of Lazica
events.summary: Gubazes II of Lazica, who had returned to the Roman alliance, accused the generals Martin and Rusticus of incompetence. In 555 Rusticus's brother John stabbed him during a meeting by the river Chobus. Justinian sent the senator Athanasius to try the killers publicly in Lazica, an exceptional judicial spectacle described by Agathias.

events.title: Samaritan and Jewish revolt at Caesarea
events.summary: In July 556 Samaritans and Jews at Caesarea Maritima, joining forces against the Christians, killed the proconsul Stephen in his praetorium. Justinian sent Amantius, who executed and mutilated the ringleaders. It followed the great Samaritan revolt of 529 and preceded another in 572.

events.title: Second plague wave in Constantinople
events.summary: In spring 558, shortly after the earthquake that cracked Hagia Sophia's dome, the bubonic plague returned to Constantinople. Agathias describes young men dying suddenly as if struck by apoplexy, noting that it had never fully left the empire since 542. Evagrius counted recurrences in roughly fifteen-year cycles.

events.title: Collapse of Hagia Sophia's first dome
events.summary: Weakened by earthquakes in December 557, the eastern part of Hagia Sophia's shallow dome collapsed on 7 May 558, crushing the altar, ambo and ciborium. Isidore the Younger, nephew of Isidore of Miletus, rebuilt it about 6 m higher with a steeper profile and 40 ribs, the dome that still stands; the church was rededicated in December 562.

events.title: The Madaba mosaic map
events.summary: A floor mosaic in a church at Madaba in Jordan, laid c. 560-565, depicts the Holy Land from Lebanon to the Nile Delta with over 150 labelled sites. Its vignette of Jerusalem shows the colonnaded cardo, the Holy Sepulchre and the Nea church, and it is the oldest surviving map of the region.

events.title: Persians and Turks destroy the Hephthalites
events.summary: Around 557-560 Khosrow I allied with the Turkic ruler Istämi to destroy the Hephthalite empire, the Turks winning the decisive battle near Bukhara. The two victors divided the Hephthalite lands along the Oxus. Persia was freed from tribute, but now bordered the more dangerous Turks.

battle.significance: Created the Turkic-Persian frontier on the Oxus.

events.title: Death of Chlothar I and the partition of 561
events.summary: Chlothar I, last surviving son of Clovis and sole king of the Franks since 558, died at Compiègne in late 561. His kingdom was partitioned by lot among his four sons: Charibert at Paris, Guntram at Orléans, Sigibert at Reims and Chilperic at Soissons, the arrangement whose rivalries Gregory of Tours chronicles.

events.title: Justinian's last heresy: aphthartodocetism
events.summary: In his final months Justinian issued an edict declaring that Christ's earthly body was incorruptible, a doctrine of Julian of Halicarnassus. Patriarch Eutychius refused and was deposed on 22 January 565; Evagrius says the emperor died before the decree could be enforced across the empire.
